pos: n. (Joseph Addison Alexander, 1809–1860, Princeton professor, orientalist, and commentator)
etymology: Greek Alexandros, defender of men; Hebrew Yoseph, he shall add.
biblical_def: Joseph Addison Alexander was the youngest son of Archibald Alexander and the most gifted linguist Princeton produced. He read Hebrew, Syriac, Arabic, Persian, Ethiopic, Sanskrit, and the modern European tongues, and he used the apparatus for one purpose: to show that the books of Scripture are what the church has always said they are. His commentary on Isaiah answered Gesenius, Hitzig, and Ewald point by point and defended the single authorship of the whole prophecy, the sixth-century reality of the Babylonian oracles, and the predictive character of the Servant passages. He wrote further commentaries on the Psalms, Acts, Mark, and part of Matthew, lectured on church history and New Testament literature, and preached with a plainness that surprised people who knew his learning. Isa 8:20 was the rule he applied to the German critics he read so thoroughly: “if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a commentary as an exposition or explanation, and philology as the study of language, its structure and etymology.
webster_full: COM'MENTARY, n. A comment, exposition or explanation of a book, or writing; annotations.
PHILOL'OGY, n. Primarily, a love of words, or a desire to know the origin and construction of language.
PROPH'ECY, n. A foretelling; prediction; a declaration of something to come.
scriptures: Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
Joh 5:39
Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me.
And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself.
corruption_summary: He mastered the German critics in their own languages and then answered them from the text.
corruption_paragraphs: The division of Isaiah into a first prophet and a Deutero-Isaiah, with a Trito-Isaiah appended, was the prestige position of continental scholarship in Alexander's lifetime and remains the default in modern academic commentary. Alexander refused it, and his refusal was not ignorance. He had read the sources, and he showed that the division rests on the prior assumption that genuine prediction does not occur. 2Ti 3:16 settles the question of what kind of book is being read: all scripture is given by inspiration, which is not a claim that survives being treated as an anthology of anonymous redactors.

The dictionary holds Alexander's position: one prophet Isaiah, one book, written in the eighth century and predicting Cyrus by name. Joh 5:39 and Luk 24:27 show Christ Himself handling the prophets as a unity that testifies of Him; a method that dissolves the books into layers cannot follow Him in that reading. Alexander's commentaries are still the model of how to take modern criticism seriously enough to dismantle it rather than merely deplore it.
usage: “To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20) — his standard for every critic he read.
“All scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2Ti 3:16) — what kind of book Isaiah is.
“they are they which testify of me” (Joh 5:39) — the unity the division destroys.

pos: n. (John Williamson Nevin, 1803–1886, German Reformed theologian, author of The Mystical Presence and The Anxious Bench)
biblical_def: John Williamson Nevin was trained at Princeton under Charles Hodge, taught at the Western Theological Seminary, and then went to the German Reformed seminary at Mercersburg, where he became the leading theologian of the movement that took its name from the place. Two of his books matter. The Anxious Bench (1843) is a sustained attack on the revival machinery of his day, arguing that the new birth comes through the ordinary ministry of word and sacrament in the church rather than through techniques designed to produce a crisis. The Mystical Presence (1846) argued that the Reformed confessions teach a real participation in the whole Christ in the Lord's Supper, and charged American Protestantism with having slid into bare memorialism. Charles Hodge reviewed it severely. 1Co 10:16 is the text Nevin pressed hardest: the cup “is it not the communion of the blood of Christ?” (1Co 10:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines communion as fellowship, and mystical as obscure, involving some secret meaning.
webster_full: COMMUN'ION, n. Fellowship; intercourse; union in faith and discipline. The body of Christians who have one common faith and discipline.
MYS'TICAL, a. Obscure; secret; remote from human apprehension; involving some secret meaning.
SAC'RAMENT, n. An oath; an ordinance instituted by Christ; a solemn religious ceremony enjoined by Christ.
scriptures: The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ?
For as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord's death till he come.
But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread, and drink of that cup.
Joh 6:37
All that the Father giveth me shall come to me; and him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.
corruption_summary: He was right that memorialism had emptied the Supper, and wrong in the direction he carried the remedy.
corruption_paragraphs: Nevin's diagnosis in The Anxious Bench deserves the dictionary's agreement. The anxious bench and its descendants substitute a procedure for the work of the Spirit, and Joh 6:37 is the answer: “All that the Father giveth me shall come to me” (Joh 6:37), which locates the efficient cause outside the method. His sacramental diagnosis is also partly right. Bare Zwinglian memorialism, which denies any spiritual presence and reduces the Supper to recollection, is not the Reformed position, and 1Co 10:16 asks a question memorialism cannot answer.

The error is where he went next. Nevin's theology of an organic, developing church life carried him toward a view of the visible institution as the continuing incarnation, and toward a liturgical and sacramental high-churchmanship that his own confessional tradition did not teach; several of his associates and his son-in-law's circle moved Romeward, and he spent years hovering. The dictionary's position is the one stated in the Lord's-Supper entry: a memorial sign and seal with Christ's true spiritual presence received by faith, neither transubstantiation nor consubstantiation nor bare memory. 1Co 11:28 keeps the ordinance where Paul put it, under self-examination by the believer, not under the mediation of a sacerdotal order.
roots_summary: Greek koinonia (G2842), communion, fellowship; dokimazo (G1381), to examine; kataggello (G2605), to declare openly.
usage: “is it not the communion of the blood of Christ?” (1Co 10:16) — his question to memorialism.
“let a man examine himself” (1Co 11:28) — where Paul puts the burden.
“All that the Father giveth me shall come to me” (Joh 6:37) — against the anxious bench.

pos: n. (Philip Schaff, 1819–1893, Swiss-German church historian in America, author of the History of the Christian Church and the Creeds of Christendom)
etymology: German surname Schaff, from Schaf, sheep, or a vessel-maker; Greek Philippos, lover of horses.
biblical_def: Philip Schaff was born in Switzerland, trained at Tübingen, Halle, and Berlin, and came in 1844 to the German Reformed seminary at Mercersburg. His inaugural address, The Principle of Protestantism, treated church history as an organic development in which the Reformation grew out of the medieval church rather than breaking with it; he was charged with heresy by his own synod and acquitted. He moved to Union Theological Seminary in New York and spent his remaining decades on the works that made him indispensable: the eight-volume History of the Christian Church, the three-volume Creeds of Christendom, the English edition of Lange's commentary, and the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series, which put the patristic corpus into English for ordinary ministers. He chaired the American committee of the Revised Version. Heb 12:23 names the company he spent his life describing, “the general assembly and church of the firstborn” (Heb 12:23).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a creed as a brief summary of the articles of Christian faith, and history as a narration of events with their causes and effects.
webster_full: CREED, n. A brief summary of the articles of Christian faith; a symbol; as the Apostles' creed.
HIST'ORY, n. A narration of events in the order in which they happened, with their causes and effects.
DEVEL'OPMENT, n. An unfolding; the discovering of something secret or withheld from notice.
scriptures: To the general assembly and church of the firstborn, which are written in heaven, and to God the Judge of all, and to the spirits of just men made perfect,
Jud 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
Eph 4:3
Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.
Gal 1:8
But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed.
corruption_summary: The greatest collector of the church's documents in English, working from a theory of history the Reformers would not have granted.
corruption_paragraphs: Schaff's documentary labour is a gift the dictionary uses constantly, and the gift is separable from the theory behind it. The theory is organic development: that the church unfolds through stages, each necessary, so that the medieval system was a proper phase and the Reformation its proper fruit. The Reformers did not describe themselves that way. They described a recovery from accumulated corruption, and Jud 1:3 gives the reason the distinction matters — the faith was “once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3), delivered complete, not grown.

The practical effect of the developmental scheme is to soften Wittenberg into a transition and to treat Rome's additions as stages rather than errors. Gal 1:8 forbids that softening: another gospel is accursed whatever its historical pedigree. Schaff's own ecumenical hope ran ahead of his evidence in the same way. The dictionary keeps his Creeds of Christendom on the shelf, uses his texts, and rejects the frame: unity is the unity of Eph 4:3 in the truth, not the convergence of traditions that still deny justification by faith alone.
roots_summary: Greek panegyris / paneguris (G3831), a general assembly; prototokos (G4416), firstborn; hapax (G530), once for all.
roots_lines: Greek hapax (G530) — once, once for all; Jude 3.
usage: “the general assembly and church of the firstborn” (Heb 12:23) — the subject of his history.
“once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3) — what development cannot improve.
“the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph 4:3) — unity in truth, not convergence.

pos: n. (the christocentric, high-sacramental and liturgical movement in the American German Reformed Church, c. 1840–1880, centred on the seminary at Mercersburg, Pennsylvania)
etymology: From Mercersburg, Pennsylvania, seat of the German Reformed seminary; theology, from Greek theos and logos.
biblical_def: Mercersburg Theology was the movement led by John Williamson Nevin and Philip Schaff and systematised by Emanuel Gerhart. Its marks were four: a christocentric dogmatics in which the incarnation, rather than the atonement alone, is the organising fact; an organic view of church history as development; a high doctrine of the Lord's Supper as real participation in the whole Christ; and a liturgical programme that produced the Order of Worship of 1866 and a long controversy with the Old Reformed party led by Joseph Berg. The movement was in revolt against two things it saw in American Protestantism — revival technique and the reduction of the sacraments to memory — and the revolt carried it past its own confessional moorings into sacerdotal and ecclesiological claims the Heidelberg Catechism does not teach. Deu 12:32 is the boundary it crossed: “thou shalt not add thereto, nor diminish from it” (Deu 12:32).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a liturgy as a form of prayers and ceremonial for public worship, and worship as the act of paying divine honors to the Supreme Being.
webster_full: LIT'URGY, n. In a general sense, all public ceremonies that belong to divine service; in a more limited sense, the common prayers and forms of divine service.
WOR'SHIP, n. Chiefly and eminently, the act of paying divine honors to the Supreme Being; or the reverence and homage paid to him in religious exercises.
ORD'INANCE, n. A rule established by authority; an institution; an established rite or ceremony.
scriptures: What thing soever I command you, observe to do it: thou shalt not add thereto, nor diminish from it.
Joh 4:24
God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.
Let all things be done decently and in order.
The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ?
corruption_summary: A right protest against memorialism and revival technique that ended in a liturgy Scripture had not commanded.
corruption_paragraphs: The movement's protest was legitimate at both points. Revival machinery does displace the ordinary means of grace, and bare memorialism does empty 1Co 10:16 of its content. Mercersburg saw this earlier and more clearly than its critics, and its sacramental writing drove American Reformed men back to Calvin and the Heidelberg Catechism, which was a real service.

The corruption is the remedy. The regulative principle of worship holds that what Scripture commands in corporate worship is required and what Scripture has not commanded is not permitted; Deu 12:32 and 1Co 14:40 together give both the restraint and the order. The Order of Worship of 1866 imported altars, responses, a church year, and a priestly conception of the minister on the authority of the church's developing life rather than of any command. Joh 4:24 names the only two requirements, spirit and truth. The dictionary takes Mercersburg's diagnosis and rejects its prescription, and notes that a movement which makes the incarnation the organising fact at the expense of the penal substitutionary atonement has shifted the centre of the gospel.
roots_summary: Greek latreia (G2999), service, worship; taxis (G5010), order; Hebrew yacaph (H3254), to add.
roots_lines: Hebrew gara' (H1639) — to diminish, take away; Deuteronomy 12:32.
usage: “thou shalt not add thereto, nor diminish from it” (Deu 12:32) — the boundary the liturgy crossed.
“worship him in spirit and in truth” (Joh 4:24) — the two requirements.
“Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40) — order, under command.

pos: n. (Emanuel Vogel Gerhart, 1817–1904, German Reformed theologian, first president of Franklin and Marshall College)
etymology: Hebrew 'Immanu'el, God with us; German surname Gerhart, spear-brave.
biblical_def: Emanuel V. Gerhart was the systematician of the Mercersburg movement. He served as first president of Heidelberg College in Ohio and then of Franklin and Marshall, and taught dogmatics at the Lancaster seminary for more than thirty years. His two-volume Institutes of the Christian Religion is the only full systematic theology the movement produced: it is organised around the person of Christ as the central fact of revelation, and derives the doctrines of the church, the sacraments, and the Christian life from the incarnation outward. He defended the Order of Worship in the liturgical controversy and he held the Heidelberg Catechism as the church's standard while reading it through the christocentric lens Nevin had supplied. Col 1:28 states his aim exactly: to “present every man perfect in Christ Jesus” (Col 1:28).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines institutes as a book of elements or principles, and dogmatical as pertaining to a dogma, positive, magisterial.
webster_full: IN'STITUTE, n. The principles of any science; a book of elements or rules; a system of principles or doctrines.
DOGMAT'ICAL, a. Positive; magisterial; asserting or disposed to assert with authority.
INCARNA'TION, n. The act of clothing with flesh; the act of assuming flesh, or of taking a human body and the nature of man.
scriptures: Col 1:28
Whom we preach, warning every man, and teaching every man in all wisdom; that we may present every man perfect in Christ Jesus:
Eph 2:20
And are built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone;
But if I tarry long, that thou mayest know how thou oughtest to behave thyself in the house of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth.
Who hath saved us, and called us with an holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace, which was given us in Christ Jesus before the world began,
corruption_summary: The one full systematic theology Mercersburg produced, built outward from the incarnation.
corruption_paragraphs: A dogmatics organised on the incarnation will tend to make the church the extension of Christ's body in a sense the New Testament does not sustain, and Gerhart's system leans that way. Eph 2:20 keeps the order right: the church is “built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets” (Eph 2:20), with Christ as the corner stone — a building resting on Him, not a continuation of Him. 1Ti 3:15 likewise makes the church the pillar and ground of the truth, a custodian rather than a source.

The dictionary does not grant the christocentric method where it displaces the covenantal and forensic categories. 2Ti 1:9 grounds salvation in God's purpose and grace given in Christ before the world began, which is election and imputation, and no system that begins with the incarnation as the organising fact handles those categories as well. Gerhart's work is a serious piece of theology and the dictionary reads it as the fullest statement of a movement whose centre was misplaced.
usage: “present every man perfect in Christ Jesus” (Col 1:28) — the aim of his dogmatics.
“built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets” (Eph 2:20) — the order his system blurs.
“according to his own purpose and grace” (2Ti 1:9) — the category he underworks.

pos: n. (Friedrich Augustus Rauch, 1806–1841, German-born first president of Marshall College, author of Psychology; or, A View of the Human Soul)
biblical_def: Frederick Rauch was a young German philosopher who left Heidelberg under political pressure, arrived in Pennsylvania in 1831, and within a few years was principal of the high school at Mercersburg and then first president of Marshall College. His Psychology; or, A View of the Human Soul, including Anthropology was the first substantial work of German idealist philosophy written in English in America. He taught that the soul is an organic unity developing through stages toward self-conscious spirit, and he used the scheme to argue against both the sensationalist psychology of the Scottish school and materialism. He died at thirty-five, and his pupils and successors at Mercersburg built on his categories. Col 2:8 is the caution the dictionary attaches to the whole enterprise: “Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit” (Col 2:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines psychology as a discourse or treatise on the human soul, and philosophy as the knowledge of the causes of all phenomena.
webster_full: PSYCHOL'OGY, n. A discourse or treatise on the human soul; or the doctrine of the nature and properties of the soul.
PHILOS'OPHY, n. Literally, the love of wisdom. In modern acceptation, the knowledge of the phenomena of nature and the causes which produce them.
SOUL, n. The spiritual, rational and immortal substance in man, which distinguishes him from brutes.
scriptures: Col 2:8
Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ.
For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. For it is written, He taketh the wise in their own craftiness.
Pro 9:10
The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom: and the knowledge of the holy is understanding.
Gen 1:1
In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.
corruption_summary: The man who brought German idealism into American Reformed divinity, and died before he could see what it did there.
corruption_paragraphs: Rauch's psychology was not written as heresy and parts of it are useful; his argument that the soul is a unity, not a bundle of faculties, is closer to the biblical anthropology than the mechanical schemes he attacked. But the developmental frame he supplied is the frame Mercersburg then applied to church history and to doctrine itself, and once development is the governing category, a corruption becomes a stage. Col 2:8 names the mechanism: a philosophy received “after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ” (Col 2:8).

The dictionary's standard is that philosophy serves exegesis or it is dismissed. 1Co 3:19 states the valuation: “the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God” (1Co 3:19), and Pro 9:10 gives the only correct starting point, the fear of the LORD. Rauch began where Hegel began, with the self-unfolding of spirit, and the men who learned from him carried the scheme into the doctrine of the church. He is a case study in how a philosophical premise outlives the man who introduced it.
roots_summary: Greek philosophia (G5385), philosophy; sulagogeo (G4812), to lead away as spoil; Hebrew yir'ah (H3374), fear, reverence.
roots_lines: Greek philosophia (G5385) — philosophy, love of wisdom; Colossians 2:8.
Greek sulagogeo (G4812) — to carry off as spoil; Colossians 2:8.
usage: “spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit” (Col 2:8) — the risk of a borrowed frame.
“the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God” (1Co 3:19) — the valuation.
“The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom” (Pro 9:10) — the right starting point.

pos: n. (Lewis Mayer, 1783–1849, first professor of the German Reformed theological seminary in America and historian of that church)
etymology: German surname Mayer, a steward or farmer; Lewis, from Germanic Hludwig, famous warrior.
biblical_def: Lewis Mayer was born in Lancaster, Pennsylvania, served German Reformed congregations in Maryland and Virginia, and in 1825 was elected the first and for some years the only professor of the newly founded German Reformed seminary, which he conducted at Carlisle and then York. He taught the whole curriculum himself, defended the Heidelberg Catechism as the church's sufficient standard, and worked at the sources of the church's own past; his History of the German Reformed Church was published after his death. He belonged to the Old Reformed party and distrusted the direction the seminary took after it moved to Mercersburg, holding that the catechism and the plain exposition of Scripture needed no philosophical reconstruction. Isa 8:20 was his instrument against innovation, and Heb 13:7 his argument for remembering the men who had taught the church before.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a catechism as a form of instruction by questions and answers, and a professor as one who publicly teaches a branch of learning.
webster_full: CAT'ECHISM, n. A form of instruction by means of questions and answers, particularly in the principles of religion.
PROFESS'OR, n. One who publicly teaches any science or branch of learning; an officer in a university or seminary.
STAND'ARD, n. That which is established by sovereign power as a rule or measure by which others are to be adjusted.
scriptures: Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
Heb 13:7
Remember them which have the rule over you, who have spoken unto you the word of God: whose faith follow, considering the end of their conversation.
The heart of the prudent getteth knowledge; and the ear of the wise seeketh knowledge.
Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.
corruption_summary: One professor, the whole curriculum, and the Heidelberg Catechism held as sufficient.
corruption_paragraphs: Mayer's career is the unglamorous half of the Mercersburg story. He built the seminary that the movement later occupied, taught alone for years, and argued that the church already possessed in the Heidelberg Catechism everything the new theology proposed to supply. Isa 8:20 is the test he applied and it is the right one: “if they speak not according to this word” (Isa 8:20), the novelty is darkness however learned.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is confessional sufficiency. A church with a sound catechism does not need a philosophical system to make it respectable, and the men who say so are usually dismissed as unlearned by the party bringing the system. Heb 13:7 commands the opposite instinct: “Remember them which have the rule over you” (Heb 13:7), and consider the end of their conversation — which is to say, look at where a teacher's doctrine actually took his pupils.
roots_summary: Hebrew torah (H8451), law, instruction; Greek mnemoneuo (G3421), to remember; anastrophe (G391), manner of life.
roots_lines: Greek anastrophe (G391) — conduct, manner of life; Hebrews 13:7.
usage: “if they speak not according to this word” (Isa 8:20) — his test for every novelty.
“Remember them which have the rule over you” (Heb 13:7) — and look where they led.
“a workman that needeth not to be ashamed” (2Ti 2:15) — one professor, whole curriculum.

pos: n. (William Buell Sprague, 1795–1876, Albany Presbyterian pastor, author of Annals of the American Pulpit and Lectures on Revivals of Religion)
etymology: English surname Sprague, from a dialect word for a lively person or a twig.
biblical_def: William B. Sprague pastored the Second Presbyterian Church of Albany for forty years and spent his spare life as the biographer of the American ministry. His nine-volume Annals of the American Pulpit gathered sketches of ministers from every major denomination in the country, built from correspondence with men who had heard them preach, and it remains a primary source for ministers of whom nothing else survives. His Lectures on Revivals of Religion (1832) is the measured Old School statement on the subject: revivals are real works of God and are to be prayed for, and the machinery that manufactures excitement is to be refused. He also assembled one of the great autograph collections of the century. Heb 13:7 is the whole programme of the Annals: remember those who spoke the word of God to you, “considering the end of their conversation” (Heb 13:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines annals as a species of history digested in the order of time, and a memoir as an account of transactions or of a person's life.
webster_full: AN'NALS, n. A species of history digested in order of time, or a relation of events in chronological order, each event being recorded under the year in which it happened.
MEM'OIR, n. A written account; a history of transactions in which one has borne a part; the history of a life.
REVI'VAL, n. Renewed attention to religion, after indifference and decline.
scriptures: Heb 13:7
Remember them which have the rule over you, who have spoken unto you the word of God: whose faith follow, considering the end of their conversation.

And I heard a voice from heaven saying unto me, Write, Blessed are the dead which die in the Lord from henceforth: Yea, saith the Spirit, that they may rest from their labours; and their works do follow them.
Pro 10:7
The memory of the just is blessed: but the name of the wicked shall rot.
I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith:
corruption_summary: Nine volumes of ministers' lives, gathered so a church would not forget who had preached to it.
corruption_paragraphs: The Annals rest on a judgment about what is worth recording. Sprague thought the ordinary pastor of an ordinary congregation was worth a careful page, and he was right; Rev 14:13 makes the ground explicit — those who die in the Lord rest from their labours, “and their works do follow them” (Rev 14:13). A denomination that keeps no such record loses the evidence of what faithful ministry looked like in its own past.

His Lectures on Revivals drew the line the dictionary draws. A revival is a sovereign work and may be sought in prayer; the protracted meeting, the anxious seat, and the engineered crisis are human substitutes that produce human results. Pro 10:7 is the quiet answer to both the forgetfulness and the showmanship: “The memory of the just is blessed: but the name of the wicked shall rot” (Pro 10:7). Sprague spent forty years writing down the first half of that verse.
roots_summary: Greek mnemoneuo (G3421), to remember; kopos (G2873), labour, toil; Hebrew zeker (H2143), memory, remembrance.
usage: “considering the end of their conversation” (Heb 13:7) — the programme of the Annals.
“and their works do follow them” (Rev 14:13) — why the record is worth keeping.
“The memory of the just is blessed” (Pro 10:7) — what he wrote down for forty years.

pos: n. (Samuel John Baird, 1817–1893, Presbyterian minister, compiler of Baird's Digest and author of The Elohim Revealed)
etymology: Scottish surname Baird, from a place name or from bard, a poet.
biblical_def: Samuel J. Baird was a Presbyterian minister who gave his working life to two kinds of labour that few men attempt. The first was documentary: his Collection of the Acts, Deliverances and Testimonies of the Supreme Judicatory of the Presbyterian Church, universally called Baird's Digest, organised more than a century of assembly actions into a usable body of ecclesiastical law, and his History of the New School traced the doctrinal course of the party that divided the church in 1837. The second was dogmatic: The Elohim Revealed in the Creation and Redemption of Man argued the realist account of original sin, that Adam's posterity were in him in a true unity of nature and so sinned in him. Charles Hodge answered it from the federal and representative side. Rom 5:12 is the ground both men stood on, that “by one man sin entered into the world” (Rom 5:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a digest as a collection or body of laws arranged under proper titles, and a testimony as a solemn declaration or affirmation.
webster_full: DIGEST, n. A collection or body of Roman laws, arranged under proper titles by order of the emperor Justinian; any collection of laws digested or arranged.
TES'TIMONY, n. A solemn declaration or affirmation made for the purpose of establishing or proving some fact.
ORIG'INAL SIN. The imputed guilt of Adam's first offense, and the corruption of nature derived from him.
scriptures: Rom 5:12
Wherefore, as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned:
Psa 51:5
Behold, I was shapen in iniquity; and in sin did my mother conceive me.
Gal 1:8
But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed.
Jud 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
corruption_summary: He catalogued a church's whole legislative memory and then argued the hardest doctrine in it.
corruption_paragraphs: The Digest sounds like clerical drudgery and is in fact a defence of order. A church whose assembly actions cannot be found will contradict itself within a generation and will have no way of knowing it has done so. Baird's History of the New School served the same end: it documented, from the record, the doctrinal steps by which an American party moved from the confession toward the New Haven account of sin and ability, so that nobody could claim the drift had not happened.

On original sin the dictionary stands with the confessional substance that Baird and his critics both defended: Rom 5:12 and Psa 51:5 teach that guilt is imputed and nature corrupted, and the realist and federal accounts are two explanations of one confessed fact. The corruption Baird fought is the one still operating — an account of sin that reduces it to individual acts, leaves the will unimpaired, and so makes grace an assistance rather than a resurrection. Jud 1:3 is why he contended in print rather than letting the matter settle itself.
roots_summary: Greek hamartia (G266), sin; dierchomai (G1330), to pass through; Hebrew 'avon (H5771), iniquity.
roots_lines: Greek dierchomai (G1330) — to pass through, pass upon; Romans 5:12.
usage: “by one man sin entered into the world” (Rom 5:12) — the ground of the whole dispute.
“I was shapen in iniquity” (Psa 51:5) — nature, not merely acts.
“earnestly contend for the faith” (Jud 1:3) — why he published rather than waited.

pos: n. (Henry Boynton Smith, 1815–1877, New School Presbyterian theologian at Union Theological Seminary, New York)
etymology: English occupational surname Smith, a worker in metal.
biblical_def: Henry Boynton Smith was converted out of Unitarian Maine, studied at Halle and Berlin under the German mediating theologians, and taught church history and then systematic theology at Union Seminary in New York for twenty-four years. He belonged to the New School party and worked to heal its breach with the Old School, which was accomplished in 1869; his address on Christian union was the instrument. His System of Christian Theology, published from his lectures after his death, organises doctrine around the incarnate Christ as the centre of all revelation and history. He held the Reformed doctrines of election and atonement while recasting them in a christocentric frame learned in Germany, and he translated and introduced much German theology to American readers. Col 1:28 describes the aim, Eph 1:4 the doctrine he would not surrender, that God “hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world” (Eph 1:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a system as a connected scheme of principles or doctrines, and union as the junction of two or more things into one.
webster_full: SYS'TEM, n. An assemblage of things adjusted into a regular whole; a connected scheme or body of doctrines.
UN'ION, n. The act of joining two or more things into one, and thus forming a compound body or a mixture; concord; agreement.
MEDIA'TION, n. Interposition; intervention; agency between parties at variance, with a view to reconcile them.
scriptures: Col 1:28
Whom we preach, warning every man, and teaching every man in all wisdom; that we may present every man perfect in Christ Jesus:
Eph 1:4
According as he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame before him in love:

Now I beseech you, brethren, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that ye all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you; but that ye be perfectly joined together in the same mind and in the same judgment.
Also of your own selves shall men arise, speaking perverse things, to draw away disciples after them.
corruption_summary: A German-trained New School theologian who held election and spent himself on reunion.
corruption_paragraphs: Smith is the best case for the New School and shows both its strength and its hazard. The strength is that he kept the substance: Eph 1:4 as unconditional choice before the foundation of the world, and an atonement that actually satisfies. The hazard is the frame. A christocentric reconstruction learned from the German mediating school tends to treat doctrinal formulations as expressions of a central life rather than as propositions to be defended, and that habit, passed to the next generation, dissolved what Smith himself held.

The reunion of 1869 was accomplished on terms that did not settle the doctrinal questions of 1837, and Act 20:30 warns where the cost falls: “of your own selves shall men arise, speaking perverse things” (Act 20:30). The dictionary values 1Co 1:10 and the labour for unity, and holds that unity which postpones the doctrinal question postpones it to a generation less able to answer it. Union Seminary's own course after Smith is the demonstration.
roots_summary: Greek eklegomai (G1586), to choose out; schisma (G4978), division, rent; diastrepho (G1294), to pervert, distort.
roots_lines: Greek eklegomai (G1586) — to choose out, elect; Ephesians 1:4.

usage: “hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world” (Eph 1:4) — what he would not give up.
“that there be no divisions among you” (1Co 1:10) — the labour of his later years.
“of your own selves shall men arise” (Act 20:30) — where a postponed question goes.
